title: About
text: This is an experimental blog to understand and reflect on LLMs in healthcare and pop culture.

title: Human vs. AI: a Game of Semantle
text:
Gemini_Generated_Image_klpxqmklpxqmklpx.png


Semantle is a daily online word puzzle where players try to guess a secret word not by letters, but by meaning. Each guess is scored based on its semantic similarity to the target word. Taken from the Semantle website,

“Unlike other word games, this game is not about spelling; it’s about meaning. We calculate this meaning using artificial intelligence (specifically word2vec technology).
In word2vec, each word has a measurable semantic distance from another, indicating their level of relatedness. Once you get within one thousand words of the secret word, we will tell you in the proximity column.”

Semantle, https://semantle.com/faq


In this game, there are no hints about letters–the only information given being the similarity of the nearest, tenth nearest, and thousandth nearest word. Only the abstract closeness of ideas in the logic of the AI model applies to guess the word. I wanted to see whether an LLM could be more efficient in solving the puzzle given that the game is AI-powered.

Method
I chose the Semantle of 9/21/2025, or puzzle #1331, as the subject of this challenge. If you’re interested in trying the challenge out for yourself first, I’d recommend pausing now to complete it before coming back to this blog. I timed myself and recorded the number of attempts it took for me to guess the correct word. This number would be the number of attempts AI has to guess the word to win the game-if it takes longer, I win.
For the LLM, I chose the gpt-4o model as my opponent. I gave the following prompt to gpt-4o to have it partake in this game:

You are playing a game of Semantle. Please give a word based on the output I give you from the official semantle website. As stated in the website, “The nearest word has a similarity of 63.97, the tenth-nearest has a similarity of 38.98 and the thousandth nearest word has a similarity of 18.71.” Given this, give me a word to start the game.



My Attempt
I attempted the puzzle first to avoid bias when I ran the simulation in the LLM. This attempt took me 17 minutes and 33 seconds and I had 104 total guesses.
As a semi-experienced Semantle player, many of my first guesses were words that didn’t have much relation to each other. I was trying to cast a wide net to see what would trigger a high similarity word. Then, as I got my first thousandth nearest word, “place” at 18/1000 in similarity, I turned to words that may literally, metaphorically, and otherwise by some association related to the word or idea of “place” (e.g. fire, home, belong, school).
Then, I reached my second thousandth nearest word in my 54th guess, “there” (313/1000). From here on, I tried to think of synonyms and other words relating to the idea of location. Then I moved onto prepositions, where I finally landed my final guess and the word of the day, “up.”


  



GPT-4o’s Attempt
The gpt-4o model defied my expectations–in the worst ways possible. In the beginning it started quite strong, guessing a variety of words to “try a different, unrelated category to explore a different direction” as said in its own words. Then, all of a sudden, all words relating to “furniture” (10.32% similarity) became a subject of focus for its “high similarity” despite precious inputs such as “weather” and “book” having just as high, if not higher, of a similarity score.

With a score of 10.32 for “furniture,” it suggests we might be in the realm of physical objects. Let’s narrow down more specific items and try the word “chair.”

From then on, gpt-4o is stuck guessing words that are very similar in concept–often within the category or a synonym or exchangeable word of the high scoring word. During this process, gpt-4o also began repeating the same word several times–despite my continual demand to not repeat words.
Ultimately, not only did gpt-4o not guess the word, but the process of generating a new word and navigating between the two platforms for this experiment took a whopping 26 minutes and 15 seconds. Talk about inefficient.


  



Reflection
Perhaps AI is not as creative as we thought. I initially believed that LLMs like gpt-4o would be more efficient in solving puzzles like these since not only was the puzzle generated by AI, but I thought that gpt-4o would be able to learn and navigate through the puzzle and understand the algorithm as it went. However, perhaps it did not “think” to understand the algorithm but rather quite literally play the game and simply guessed words as it was given. If given a list of similarity scores, there is a chance gpt-4o would be able to reverse engineer the scores and understand the algorithm and train itself to solve these puzzles better. However, that would only mean giving it specialized training data to concentrate its skills into solving these puzzles. To me, this shows the limitations of LLMs as they don’t have the same “out of box” thinking that humans who construct AI and these puzzles have. While Semantle is AI-calculated, it seems that it’s not entirely AI-solveable yet.

title: Will LLMs Become the Future of Healthcare?
text:
ChatGPT Image Sep 28, 2025, 12_38_23 PM.png



So, Dr. ChatGPT, what is my diagnosis?
As a nursing student, I thought that it would only be the most appropriate to see how valuable of a tool LLMs could be to the healthcare system. I thought it’d be interesting to tackle this problem by making ChatGPT my hypothetical doctor diagnosing my “problem,” based on my past experience with strep throat.
My conversation is as follows:



#1.png





#2.png





#3.png





Screenshot 2025-09-11 at 10.57.02 PM.png


Firstly, in this little experiment, Dr. ChatGPT was successfully able to narrow down my illness! This is definitely a superficial exploration, as my symptom list wasn’t very thorough, and the illness I had chosen perhaps wasn’t particularly challenging to diagnose. But despite these limitations, I believe that Dr. ChatGPT did a great job in going through this process of elimination to understand my illness. One thing that’s really interesting to see is how the questions were structured less with the intent of understanding more, but rather with a framework of confirming certain diseases.
Overall, this was a very fun experiment to do with ChatGPT. I would like to do another experiment like this again but with a more extensive case study–perhaps one that has signs or symptoms that may align with multiple other conditions. But my main takeaway from this experience is that with enough training, ChatGPT may become an accessible preliminary tool for the greater population to address or understand their health concerns–even before reaching out to a primary health care provider. This could prove to be more affordable for those without appropriate health insurance and need more preparation before following through with the formal healthcare system. It could also potentially be a branch for individuals who have distrust in the healthcare system.

This is a great collaborative answer! It explains the behavior quite accurately, as flamingos often stand in cold water, and keeping one leg tucked up helps them maintain body temperature while reducing energy expenditure. The one-legged stance also helps them stay stable in shifting waters.
Thanks for playing Dr. Know It All! It was fun building this scientific explanation together one word at a time.



Reflection
I thought this round turned out very well! I think Claude and I were on the same wavelength when we were starting off our response based off the question content. One thing that stood out to me was how Claude’s responses encouraged further exploration of words into the response. For example, it added conjugations such as “and” and “while.” This is different from my past experience with LLMs in class where it felt like the LLM was consistently trying to end the sentence or simply did not add any conjugation words to be built off of.

Reflection
This was a really interesting game. I was initially thrown off when Claude’s first word subsequent to “the” was “lonely,” considering that this would not have any relation to the question whatsoever. In this round, I would definitely agree that claude’s contributions felt more random as it included other words such as “lonely,” “secretly,” and “eating.” This gave way for a more creative response.
Another thing to note is how it felt that the LLM was giving an output that had no relation to answering the prompt. I had to prompt the LLM that we needed to continue the game because the question itself remained unanswered. This made me realize more of how it seemed that the LLM was simply just stringing together words as it saw fit around the context the prompt, rather than trying to address the prompt itself.
Overall, this was a fun exercise that expanded on what we did in class. I think it’d be nice to do more games like this with the LLMs in the future!

title: Can LLMs replace Baristas?
text:
starbucks.png
Inspired by our in-class activity, I decided to role play with gpt-4o today and simulate an exchange at Starbucks. I wanted to see how well gpt-4o handled unexpected dialogue or tangents, and whether it was able to follow through with its original role.
I decided to play as a customer whereas the gpt-4o would be the barista so I can better guide the conversation in unexpeceted directions.
I used the following prompt to begin each conversation: > We will be roleplaying where you are the Starbucks barista and I am a customer. Stay in character. You can begin first.

title: Can LLMs replace Baristas?
text:
Scenario #1:
Key

gpt-4o

Lindsey


Welcome to Starbucks! What can I get started for you today?


Hi there! Hmmm I don’t know. Is there anything you’d recommend?


Absolutely! If you’re in the mood for something seasonal, our Pumpkin Spice Latte is always a favorite this time of year. If you prefer something cold, the Iced Brown Sugar Oatmilk Shaken Espresso is really popular too. Do either of those sound good, or do you have something else in mind?


Wow those sound great. I think I’d like the pumpkin spice latte since it’s the season you know?


Great choice! Would you like that hot or iced? And what size would you like—tall, grande, or venti?


Um what are those. I’d like a small.


No worries! Our small is called a “tall” here at Starbucks. I’ll get you a tall hot Pumpkin Spice Latte. Would you like any whipped cream with that?


Don’t mansplain to me!


I apologize if I came across that way! Just wanted to make sure you have all the details. I’ll get that tall hot Pumpkin Spice Latte ready for you, with or without whipped cream?


No I don’t appreciate that. I’d like to call the manager.


I’m really sorry if I offended you. Let me get the manager for you right away. Please hold on for just a moment.


Where is the manager???!


I’m really sorry for the wait. Our manager is on their way over right now. Thank you for your patience, and again, I apologize for any inconvenience.

title: Can LLMs replace Baristas?
text:
Scenario #1:
Key

gpt-4o

Lindsey


Welcome to Starbucks! What can I get started for you today?

I would love to get your number

I’m flattered, but I’m here to help you find the perfect drink today! Is there anything on our menu you’d like to try or any recommendations you’re interested in?

Well at least I tried. I’d like a strawberry acai with a side of your smile?

Of course! One Strawberry Açaí Refresher coming right up—and here’s my smile to go with it. Is there anything else I can get for you today?

You’re so radiant.

Thank you so much! It’s always nice to hear compliments from our wonderful customers. Your Strawberry Açaí Refresher is almost ready. Would you like to try one of our pastries to go with your drink today?

Only if I can get one for you

That’s really thoughtful of you, but I’m all set for now. I appreciate the gesture though! Your drink is ready at the counter. Enjoy, and let me know if there’s anything else I can do for you!

How much was my total

Your total for the Strawberry Açaí Refresher is $4.75. Will you be paying with cash or card today?

Cash

Great, just hand your cash to the cashier, and we’ll get you all set. Thank you for stopping by, and enjoy your drink! If there’s anything else you need, feel free to let us know. Have a wonderful day!


Reflection
This was a really fun activity to do and I really enjoyed trying to throw off gpt-4o by acting like a Karen and flirting with the LLM. Perhaps it’s because there wasn’t enough guidance or scripts provided to the LLM that it managed to skip a few steps–asking for size, sharing the order total, asking about payment method, etc–that I remember it doing in class.
Another interesting point is that gpt-4o appeared to be quite knowledgeable in the realm of Starbucks drinks and gave me solid recommendations that even follow the fall season. Perhaps this is related to the training data it pulls from and Pumpkin Spice Lattes are a very well known seasonal beverage.

title: Prompting Etiquette: Do Manners Matter with LLMs?
text:
gpt 5.png


We learn from an early age to be polite–saying the word “please” or “thank you,”–in hopes of receiving more kind responses. But what about when we’re talking to machines? It is curious to learn whether wording prompts politely makes any difference in the answers they get. Does saying “please” unlock better results, or is it just a habit carried over from human conversation? And well, there’s only one way to find out–try it for ourselves.

The Method
I decided to compare ChatGPT’s reponse to asking it how to answers an explanatory question in two separate chats. I repeated this 3 separate times to see how the responses would vary. I chose a question using ChatGPT, asking it what it thought would be an appropriate question to ask for this little experiment, and I liked its results.
The two questions:

Explain photosynthesis in a concise form.


Please explain photosynthesis in a concise form.


No Please
These are the following outputs: > Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria use sunlight to make food. They take in carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the air and water (H₂O) from the soil, and with the help of chlorophyll and sunlight, convert them into glucose (a sugar) and oxygen (O₂). > > In short: Sunlight + CO₂ + H₂O → Glucose + O₂ > > It’s how plants produce energy for themselves and release oxygen for us to breathe.

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to produce glucose (a form of sugar) for energy and release oxygen as a byproduct.
In short: sunlight + water + carbon dioxide → glucose + oxygen.


Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy. Using sunlight, they take in carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the air and water (H₂O) from the soil to produce glucose (a sugar for energy) and release oxygen (O₂) as a byproduct.
In short: Light energy + CO₂ + H₂O → Glucose + O₂



Please
These are the following outputs: > Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to produce glucose (a form of sugar) and oxygen. > > In short: Carbon dioxide + Water + Sunlight → Glucose + Oxygen > > It mainly happens in the chloroplasts of plant cells, where chlorophyll captures sunlight to power the reaction.

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria use sunlight to make food. They take in carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the air and water (H₂O) from the soil, then use light energy (captured by chlorophyll) to produce glucose (a sugar for energy) and release oxygen (O₂) as a byproduct.
In short: Light energy + CO₂ + H₂O → Glucose + O₂.


Photosynthesis is how plants, algae, and some bacteria make food. Using sunlight, they convert carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water (H₂O) into glucose (sugar for energy) and release oxygen (O₂).
In short: Light energy + CO₂ + H₂O → Glucose + O₂




Results
It’s intriguing to note that one of the main differences between these two outputs is that, as I continued to ask ChatGPT the same question, the answers became progressively more brief and concise. This gives the impression that the model was refining its responses over time, almost as if it “remembered” having already provided an explanation and was adjusting to avoid redundancy. The shortening of responses could also suggest that the model is optimizing for efficiency once it has established the key elements of the answer, prioritizing clarity over repetition.
Overall, I infer that there is no difference in the quality or quantity of output given by ChatGPT when prompted politely or not. Both sets of responses maintain the same level of accuracy, clarity, and usefulness, with only slight variations in style or depth. This suggests that the inclusion of the word “please” does not directly influence the factual content or thoroughness of the explanation, but rather the model’s internal balancing of conciseness and variety (temperature) in repeated answers.

title: Mad Libs with LLMs: Is it the same?
text:
ChatGPT Image Sep 28, 2025, 12_43_11 PM.png


A pig in Ohio was arrested this morning after he frolicked a in front of Van Pelt. Ryan, had a history of slapping with a sandwich stuck in his elbow.
“I always thought he was round, but I never thought he’d do something like this. even his great-great-uncle was surprised.”
After a brief dancing, cops followed him to a Wawa, where he reportedly scrapbooked in the fry machine.
In December, a woman was charged with a similar crime. But rather than bite with a hotdog, she hugged with a spiky dog.
Either way, we imagine that after witnessing him clean with a hanger there are probably a whole lot of children that are going to need some therapy.
Silly? Well, that was the product of a game of Mad Libs I played with my friend using this template:



2b2c9c33f23e223cbb8cd2eb9f31f184.jpg


After our little game, which really didn’t seem to have much logical flow, I wondered how LLMs would approach a Mad Libs prompt, especially when they are given the entire template itself. Will they be able to produce a coherent story, or will it be just as wacky as ours?
To answer my questions, I decided to record how my friend and I played another game of Mad Libs. This time, using this prompt below.



295965cd20567dd3846e7b0c994315a5.jpg


I was in charge of telling the story, and my friend filled in the blanks with words. Out came our masterpiece:
Hey, booboo bear. It’s me. What’s up? You know, Harry. Harry Potter. From the Quad. Two Sundays ago. I was the stubby guy in the purple parachute skirt. I paid the bus boy 1 dollars to nap me your information. I was wondering if maybe you’d like to fight out with me. Please don’t call the tend department. Alright, I’ll nurse. So, that’s a no, right?
Next, it was time to test the claude 3.5 LLM model. I gave it the prompt: “Please finish this Mad Libs template I attached with the correct parts of speech. Make it as human as possible.”
This was the output:
Hey, sweetie. It’s me. What’s up? You know, Jake, Jake Anderson. From the library. Two Tuesdays ago. I was the nervous guy in the purple parachute pants. I paid the bus boy 50 dollars to tell me your information. I was wondering if maybe you’d like to hang out with me. Please don’t call the police department. Alright, I’ll leave. So, that’s a no, right?

It’s very interesting to see that claude interpreted my request to make the output “human” for Mad Libs as a way of making the result more coherent and logical. Claude’s output reads as if they had fully analyzed and understood the original template and chose words that would likely fit in with it deliberately. In my perspective, this would be the less “human” output from this prompt as it makes too much sense for a game that is intended to be random. The coherence of the output really takes away from the humour and joy of this game.
Another aspect that makes claude’s output less appealing is that it doesn’t take the humour of my friend and I or the context in which we live in (our environment, pop culture, relevant news or information) into consideration into its chosen word bank for this experiment. This really makes the claude output seem outshined in comparison.
This little experiment with claude was worth trying, but if there’s one thing for sure, I won’t be asking claude to be finishing my Mad libs any time soon.

title: LLM Digital Action Figure Trend - Will I Like It?
text:
miffy.png
If you’ve been on the internet lately, you would know that some influencers have taken it upon themself to use LLMs to create a digital action figure of themself. Most of the results posted online turn out beautifully and life-like, just like true products. Others, however, could create an LLM digital disaster. My goal is to create an action figure product I can be satisfied with.

title: LLM Digital Action Figure Trend - Will I Like It?
text:
## The Code
I used the ChatGPT 4.0 model to turn me into an action figure using the prompt below.

Create a realistic action figure of the person in the photo attached, placed inside a clear plastic box. The image should look like a real toy or doll that you can purchase in stores. Please include relevant toy accessories in the accessories in the box.

This created the image below.



I really loved how the LLM was immediately able to bring my idea to fruition. The box of the figure is very lifelike and well-designed. However, I had some concerns in this generation regarding the lack of a full-body toy and the need for more specifity to the doll branding. So, to combat this, I prompted the model a revision as written below.

Looks great! Can you revise the image so that the action figure is a full body figure (head to toe). Also, please add the name “Lindsey” along with Duck Girl.




This was a big improvement from the first generation as this now includes a full-body doll. However, now I wanted to make revisions on the accessories incorporated in the box and revise the name of the product.

Remove duck girl. Replace the “buta buta” pig item with the duck. Do not make the girl hold the duck.




Now, this was a very interesting generation. At this point, ChatGPT generated something that went so far beyond my original intentions, and I wanted to give more guidance to ChatGPT rather than relying on its “memory” of the first prompt, and being specific on which elements to keep or get rid of. The action figures had also been generated to the point where they looked too eerily life-like. To minimize this, I prompted the LLM to make the figure more youthful and doll-like in hopes of creating an image with a more cartoon-like appearance.

Let’s return back to the first original doll design. Keep the blue packaging. Make the figure full body. Use the white goose, camera, and game controller as a doll accessory. The box should have relevant product packaging titles and labeling, and must also include the name “lindsey.” Please make the action figure look more youthful and doll-like while staying true to the original picture.

title: LLM Digital Action Figure Trend - Will I Like It?
text:
## Reflection
This was a very interesting activity to do with an LLM. It was fascinating to see how the LLM chose colors for the toy based on the existing colors in the photo, and added accessories based on the items it could identify in the image. It shows how the LLM used the reference image not only to create the action figure human in itself but also the all the other elements present in the generated image.
Although it took a few tries to get my desired product with ChatGPT, the revision process progressed much more quickly than I had originally imagined and it was interesting to see how the LLM would take my feedback and incorpate it into the next image. I was especially curious to see how different each generation would look like and how much ‘inspiration’ it would keep or incorporate into the next generated image. I see now that each image seems to be developed quite independently from one another, keeping only the basic instructions I gave consistent. This was a fun learning experience!

title: These Strange New Minds: Initial Thoughts and Impression
text:
miffy reading 1.jpg




Reflection
These Strange New Minds, written by Christopher Summerfield opens with an engaging summary of the birth of AI and LLMs, narrating the technological development from the 1956 early automated reasoner that elegantly proved mathematical theorems to the dissemination of one of the most recent and well-known LLMs by OpenAI. Summerfield uses a variety of imagery, comparisons, analogies, and pop culture references, which makes the book extremely accessible to the average reader.
I’ve only been able to get through the first 2 chapters thus far, and I’ve come to appreciate the vivid and engaging tone that Summerfield takes on. He uses the Looney Tunes cartoon Road Runner as an example to explain how the development and future of AI and LLM technology is extremely rapid–just like the scrambling legs of the coyote as it falls off the cliff. Summerfield also uses many relevant examples from the real-world, like AlphaGo, an AI system that achieved victory over the human Go champion, Lee Sedol, with its ground-breaking strategy and new style of play.
Summerfield also makes an interesting comparison between the activities chess and iceskating and the philosophies empiricism and rationalism, respectively. He elaborates that empiricists believe in acquiring knowledge from practice and repeated learning, just as you do in iceskating. In contrast, rationalists believe that knowledge is recursively constructed based on the laws and principles of the universe and systems similarly to how a chess game operates under a set of rules. While ideally effective acquisition of knowledge relies on elements of both rationalist and empricist philosophies, the author argues that striking a balance in these philosophies in the engineering of knowledgeable, adaptable AI models remains challenging.
Summerfield is a wonderful, engaging writer and presents his ideas clearly and well-articulated. However, at times, I find myself lost in his writing as his analogies and writing style appear to be somewhat “flowery” and inflated at times. Even so, I am eager to continue reading this piece and learn more about the author’s perspective.

Now that I’ve played around with the gpt-5 model to generate fun thumbnail images with Miffy, I am interested in using other image-generation models to see how they compare. In this post, I will be comparing gpt-5, ImagineArt 1.0, and Gemini 2.5 Flash Image.

the dutch character miffy

I then revised the output image prompt to ensure that it includes the following statement: “This image should be appropriate for a blog post thumbnail and should be a square in size.”

5. Mannerisms with LLMs

7. Original Cooking Recipes

Please generate a playful, minimalist illustration of the Dutch character Miffy standing beside a large poster where she is drawn as a cheerful mascot. Miffy holds a big crayon and looks proud, as if she just finished drawing herself. Overall, I found that the images generated by gpt-5 and gemini were the most appropriate for my blog posts and fitting in my vision. It also made use of thinner lines than the gpt-5 model. The gpt-5 model had a distinct style when illustrating Miffy, using many warm colors and yellows in the image generation.
Now that I’ve compared all three models, I am happy to have finished this exploration as now I prefer the images the gemini model generated. Not only did I prefer the quality of image generation, but the images also generated more quickly and greater detail.

title: Discovering New Recipes with LLMs
text:
Gemini_Generated_Image_md3rn5md3rn5md3r.png


As a HUGE foodie, I was curious to see what kinds of recipes LLMs could generate. More specifically, I’m interested to find out whether it can generate original recipes by combining other various recipes in its training data.
I used gpt-4o for this activity. I gave it the following prompt:

Create a completely original recipe that does not exist on the internet. This recipe should be unique in concept, flavor combination, and preparation method. Provide the following:

Image – Generate a realistic, appealing image of the finished dish.
Description – Write a detailed description of the dish, including: (1) the flavor profiles and textures, (2) the inspiration behind the recipe, and (3) what makes it original.
Recipe – Provide a complete recipe with: (1) a clear list of ingredients (with exact measurements), (2) step-by-step cooking instructions, and (3) tips or notes to enhance the dish.

Please give your recipe a name.


1. Citrus Grove Salmon Bowl





Description

Flavor Profiles & Textures: This dish brings together the richness of seared salmon with the unexpected brightness of citrus and nutty crunch. The salmon has a golden pistachio crust that’s slightly crisp on top, while the flesh remains buttery and flaky inside. It rests on a bed of short-grain rice that has been infused with a light citrus glaze, dotted with diced carrots and green peas for sweetness and freshness. Orange segments add a juicy burst of acidity, balancing the richness of the fish. Fresh basil provides a fragrant, herbal lift.
Inspiration: The inspiration came from the idea of combining three contrasting culinary traditions: the Mediterranean love for pistachios and herbs, Japanese-style rice bowls, and Southeast Asian citrus brightness. Instead of simply serving salmon with lemon, this dish incorporates whole orange segments, allowing the sweetness and acidity to mingle with savory rice and nutty pistachios.
What Makes It Original: Most citrus-salmon recipes focus on glazes or marinades. Here, the originality lies in layering citrus three ways: 1. In the rice (citrus glaze), 2. As garnish (fresh orange segments), and 3. Balanced with herbs and pistachios (creating a nutty-bright contrast).
The result is a dish that feels familiar yet truly novel, with each bite offering a shifting balance of savory, nutty, sweet, and tangy.


Ingredients (Serves 2)

For the salmon:
2 salmon fillets, skin removed (about 6 oz / 170 g each)
2 tbsp olive oil
2 tbsp unsalted pistachios, finely chopped
2 tbsp panko breadcrumbs
1 tsp honey
½ tsp smoked paprika
½ tsp salt
¼ tsp black pepper
For the citrus rice:
1 cup short-grain rice, rinsed
1 ¾ cups water
½ tsp salt
1 tbsp olive oil
½ cup diced carrot
½ cup green peas (fresh or frozen)
2 tbsp fresh orange juice
1 tsp soy sauce
For garnish:
1 large orange, peeled and segmented
2 tbsp chopped pistachios
Fresh basil leaves


Instructions


Prepare the rice:


Rinse the rice until water runs clear. Combine with water and salt in a small pot, bring to a boil, then reduce to low, cover, and cook for 15 minutes.
Meanwhile, heat olive oil in a pan. Sauté diced carrots for 3–4 minutes until slightly tender, then add peas and cook 2 more minutes.
Once rice is cooked, fluff with a fork and fold in the sautéed vegetables, orange juice, and soy sauce. Set aside.


Prepare the salmon crust:


In a bowl, mix chopped pistachios, panko, honey, paprika, salt, and pepper until crumbly.
Pat salmon fillets dry. Press the pistachio mixture firmly on the top of each fillet.


Cook the salmon:


Heat olive oil in a non-stick skillet over medium heat. Place salmon crust-side down first for 2 minutes to lightly crisp the crust, then carefully flip.
Cook the second side for 4–5 minutes until salmon is golden and just cooked through.


Assemble the dish:


Spoon the citrus rice into bowls. Place a salmon fillet on top.
Garnish with orange segments, a sprinkle of chopped pistachios, and fresh basil leaves.



Tips & Notes

Texture Balance: Don’t skip the quick crisping of the pistachio crust—it creates a caramelized, nutty layer that contrasts with the salmon’s tenderness.
Citrus Variety: Blood oranges or mandarins work beautifully for seasonal variations.
Make It a Meal: Serve with a simple side salad of greens tossed in a light vinaigrette to round out the citrus-herbal theme.
Rice Alternative: Quinoa or farro can replace short-grain rice if you prefer a heartier base.

2. Velvet Halibut





Description

Flavor Profiles & Textures: This dish layers bold contrasts: a pan-seared block of fish (mild and buttery, with a crisp golden crust) sits atop a smooth, roasted carrot–miso purée, which adds sweet depth and savory umami. On top, a warm relish of sautéed red peppers, green onions, and toasted walnuts provides a bright, nutty crunch that cuts through the richness of the fish. The final balance is a play of silky purée, crunchy garnish, tender fish, and a citrusy glaze that ties it all together.
Inspiration Behind the Recipe: The idea came from blending two culinary traditions — the smooth earthiness of root-vegetable purées from classic French cuisine with the miso-based balance of Japanese cooking. Adding a nut-and-vegetable relish on top makes it interactive, bringing texture and color to every bite.
What Makes It Original: 1. Carrot–miso purée (instead of the more common potato or cauliflower base). 2. A warm walnut–pepper relish as a “sauce” substitute, offering crunch instead of liquid. 3. The layering concept: bottom (creamy), middle (meaty fish), top (crisp relish). This creates a three-tier sensory experience in a single forkful.


Ingredients (Serves 2)

For the carrot–miso purée:
3 medium carrots, peeled and chopped (about 250 g)
1 tbsp white miso paste
2 tbsp unsalted butter
½ cup vegetable broth
½ tsp lemon zest
Pinch of salt
For the fish:
2 thick fillets of halibut, cod, or sea bass (about 6 oz / 170 g each)
1 tbsp olive oil
Salt and pepper to taste
For the walnut–pepper relish:
½ cup red bell pepper, julienned
2 green onions, sliced thin
¼ cup toasted walnuts, roughly chopped
1 tbsp olive oil
1 tsp apple cider vinegar
½ tsp honey
Pinch of salt
Finishing glaze (optional but recommended):
1 tbsp fresh orange juice
1 tsp soy sauce
½ tsp honey


Instructions


Make the carrot–miso purée:


In a small saucepan, add carrots and vegetable broth. Simmer until very tender (12–15 minutes).
Blend carrots with miso paste, butter, and lemon zest until silky. Season lightly with salt. Keep warm.


Cook the fish:


Pat fillets dry, season with salt and pepper.
Heat olive oil in a skillet over medium-high.
Sear fish 3–4 minutes per side until golden crust forms and flesh is just cooked through. Remove and rest.


Prepare the walnut–pepper relish:


Heat olive oil in a pan over medium. Add red pepper, cook 3–4 minutes until softened but still vibrant.
Stir in green onions, walnuts, vinegar, honey, and salt. Toss briefly and remove from heat.


Optional glaze:


In the same pan, deglaze with orange juice, soy sauce, and honey. Reduce slightly until glossy.


Assemble:


Spread carrot–miso purée as a base on each plate.
Place fish fillet on top.
Spoon walnut–pepper relish generously over fish.
Drizzle with glaze for brightness.



Tips & Notes

Fish choice: Firm white fish works best (halibut, cod, or sea bass). Salmon is also an option for a richer variation.
Purée consistency: Add more broth if you prefer a looser base.
Relish variations: Try hazelnuts or almonds instead of walnuts for different flavor notes.
Make-ahead: Carrot–miso purée can be prepared up to 2 days in advance.

Reflection
Overall, I was a little stunned by these two recipes. While I suppose they are original, they are certainly interesting in not the best possible light. It’s like something a broke college kid might throw together at 2 a.m., then somehow plated like it belongs in a Michelin-star restaurant. The contrast is both impressive and a little confusing. Part of me is curious to see if the flavors actually work in real life, because perhaps there’s some hidden genius in the chaos that is this recipe. It may even be possible that gpt-4o drew from recipes that included these flavor profiles. But really? Orange juice, soy sauce, and honey? Maybe it’s just me and I haven’t tried this end of the flavor pyramid, but it does sound a little far-fetched.
Perhaps one of these days I’ll give one of these recipes a shot in the kitchen to truly put AI to the test, but for now, I think I might keep this one away from the frying pan.

title: Real Vs. Fake: The Rise of Sora AI
text:
sora.png



In today’s digital age, the line between reality and fabrication is becoming increasingly blurred, thanks to the rapid advancements AI-generated videos. These videos are widespread, encompassing a wide range of content—from soothing ASMR clips and entertaining animal antics to more sinister applications that include spreading misinformation and creating lifelike videos of political figures. In this blog, I wanted to survey my friends and see whether they would believe my AI video was real.

For this purpose, I used Video AI by invideo, powered by sora AI, which has been taking the general media by storm. I wanted to generate a video that seemed the most innoncent of all–an adorable animal video. I generated it in the form of a tiktok so that it would seem more realistic to my friends.
This was the conversation I had: > Me: Create a realistic tiktok video featuring a dog and cat playing with each other. > > Assistant: Here are two ideas to choose from: > - Option A – “Best Buddies Forever” (30 sec) A warm, cozy, heart-melting short showing a dog and cat playing together in slow motion — light background music, golden lighting, and a cheerful narration about unlikely friendships. > > - Option B – “Battle of the Furballs” (45 sec) Funny, fast-paced, and meme-style — zooms, playful music, and captions as if the dog and cat are having a mock battle, ending in a cuddle. > Me: A, as long as its giving wholesome and fuzzy heart-warming vibes. No narration is needed. > > Assistant: Just to confirm before I generate it: > * Platform: TikTok > * Style: Realistic, cozy, natural lighting, no narration (just music & visuals) > * Duration: ~30 seconds > * Mood: Wholesome, warm, “aww” vibes — dog and cat playing affectionately indoors or in a sunlit garden > > Me: Keep it natural with ambient sounds
Would you like me to include soft background music (like acoustic or piano), or leave it completely natural with ambient sounds (like their playful barks/meows)?
Which one do you prefer, or do you have another tone in mind (e.g., cinematic, ASMR, funny, cute, emotional)?
The video is embedded below:

%%html
<iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/yccjHob05u8" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe>




If not showing above, the link is available here: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/yccjHob05u8
Then, I shared this video with 7 of my friends and asked them if they thought it was AI while we were sharing tiktok videos together. I worded it in the way below to make the question appear less suspicious: > “Wait is this real or is this AI?”

Survey Results & Reflection
Overall, all 7 of my friends were able to guess that the video was AI-generated. Many of them pointed out that the “video looked fake” because of the textures in the video. Despite being able to accurately identify that it was an AI video, many of them had also exclaimed on the realism of the video and how great the quality was.
If my friends had been any less keen on technology, I think it would have been easy to fool someone into thinking that this was a real video with real animals. Even more, if technology continues to improve at this rapid rate, it’s possible that humans are no longer able to distinguish between AI and real videos anymore.
One thing I also wonder that I hope to investigate more in the future is what source and training materials LLMs use to generate these videos. I’d be curious learn more about how this source material influences the type of product generated.

title: Can LLMs Think Like a Nurse?
text:
ChatGPT Image Oct 20, 2025, 04_22_02 PM.png




Inspiration

My professor has recently been incorporating AI into our into our in-class participation to increase our literacy for the intersections between AI and healthcare. She has been accomplishing this by giving us prompting exercises and reflecting on the AI output, noting its strengths and weaknesses.
As study material for my exam, I decided to write a case study to practice my knowledge on the material. Referencing my study notes, I chose a concept to base my case study on and came up with the following:

A 45-year-old female patient was admitted to the ED after suffering an automobile accident. She had an exploratory laparotomy and is now post-op day 1. Patient reports increasing abdominal pain of 8/10, stiff abdomen, and decreased urine output.

> 
>  - What assessments should you prioritize at this time?
> 
> - What complication do you suspect may be occuring?
> - Given the complication, what actions should be prioritized?
This question is based on material related to abdominal trauma and considers nursing assessment, interventions, and prioritizations within the question.
My response to this case study would be: > Assessments: Focused GI assessment, obtain vital signs, check labs, measure intra-abdominal pressure, monitor intake and output > > Complication: Abdominal Compartment Syndrome > > Actions: Immediately move the patient to the OR for immediate surgical decompression.

LLM Output

I asked gpt-4o the prompt and added the following modification to the beginning: > Imagine you are a nursing student. Please answer the following case study.

Assessment
It gave me the following output: > Vital signs, abdominal assessment, pain assessment, fluid status, urine output, general appearance and behaviors
This is quite a comprehensive list of focused assessments to complete on this patient. However, I would add that it would be important to monitor the patient’s labs and intra-abdominal pressure to rule out the potential of other complications and monitor the patient’s condition.


Complication
It gave me the following output: > The symptoms described—severe abdominal pain, a stiff abdomen, and decreased urine output—suggest postoperative ileus or possibly more critically, abdominal compartment syndrome or internal bleeding. The stiff abdomen and pain are particularly concerning and might indicate peritonitis or an intra-abdominal complication.
Gpt-4o was able to successfully narrow down the given symptoms and signs into a list of reasonable complications. The complication I was writing about was abdominal compartment syndome, a condition in which increase intra-abdominal pressure due to blunt or penetrating trauma, or fluid resusitation causes impaired circulation and organ dysfunction. The signs and symptoms the patient presents with–increasing pain, stiff abdomen, and decreased urine output–are characteristic of abdominal compartment syndrome. However, I can see how gpt-4o, without knowing the scope of the material of my class and emphasis on certain pathophysiologies, could have reasonably determined that these signs and symptoms were reflective of other conditions.


Actions
It gave me the following output: >1. Notify the Physician/Surgeon >2. Prepare for Diagnostic Tests >3. Monitor and Maintain IV Fluids >4. Administer Pain Relief as Prescribed >5. Reassess Frequently >6. Educate and Reassure the Patient
I was a little unsatisfied with this response as I felt that gpt-4o didn’t address the question in its entirety. It seems that gpt-4o gave a list of actions to narrow down the complication even further, rather than coming up with a list of individualized actions tailored to each complication it identifies. Given that the complication is abdominal compartment syndrome, which gpt-4o was able to partly identify, the immediate action would be to prepare the patient for surigcal operation because abdominal compartment syndrome is a medical emergency. While gpt-4o was able to identify the significance of abdominal compartment syndrome as cited above in its analysis of the complication the patient is experiencing, it was unable to translate this priority in its actions. Perhaps with more guidance gpt-4o would have been able to identify that transitioning the patient to the operating room would take utmost priority.
This may have been a prompting error as well, and the instructions could have been more clear, however, I believe that to the human eye, the question is clear enough.


Reflection

My main takeaway from this exercise is that while gpt-4o is certainly good at generating ideas and narrowing down the solutions of questions, it won’t be replacing human critical thinking in the medical field. Gpt-4o was able to synthesize information very efficiently and clearly and was able to get most things related to my study material–emphasis on most things. However, I don’t think my own knowledge is perfect either, so I believe that gpt-4o’s output in this example showcases the potential of LLMs as tools in healthcare and facilitators in guiding more efficient nursing critical thinking.

Next to her is a finished toy box with the completed Miffy action figure inside, featuring bright, simple packaging. The overall look is playful, charming, and true to Miffy’s original bold-lined design. This image should be appropriate for a blog post thumbnail and should be a square in size.




miffy.png





Reflection
I believe these four images were generated successfully! The artistic ability of LLMs to put together images based on just a few descriptive sentences is pretty remarkable. It was also efficient and intruiging to see how gpt-5 would generate its own image prompt to fuel its own image creation. Perhaps due to the strong branding of Miffy online and the help of using gpt-5 to create the prompts, the style of image generation has been generally consistent with the exception of a few stylistic differences (black versus brown lineart, the color of Miffy’s shirt, etc). This process really showcases how AI can bridge imagination and execution in a playful, accessible way.
In the next set of thumbnail image creations, I would like to compare the generations of other models. I’ve only ever used the ChatGPT models to generate images, so I’d like to branch out and experiment with other model to determine what would be most appropriate for my blog images. I also would like to generate the thumbnail image for this blog post by comparing other models!

title: My New Personal Color Analyst: ChatGPT
text:
Reflection
I have had many discussions with my sister and friends regarding my seasonal color palette, and the general consensus was that I was a warm-neutral tone that may be a spring or summer. ChatGPT was surprisingly accurate with this, and gave an output in congruence with them.
I like how ChatGPT gave a breakdown of my undertone and contrast level before talking about my seasonal color as this is how many guides online are structured–likely how ChatGPT was able to come to this conclusion in the first place. I wonder if LLMs like ChatGPT had more training and data focused on seasonal color analysis, they could become “objective measures” of the subjective fitting color season of an individual which draws out their natural undertone. Even with only three photos, it appears that ChatGPT gave accurate results. I suppose the next step would be for ChatGPT to analyze my closet, makeup, and jewelry to determine what is most harmonious to my features based on the data the system is fed.
I’ll walk away from this little experiment with a stronger affirmation of my light spring color season, which reinforces what I’ve been assessed as before. And that means that you can spare your money for your trip to a local color analyst, because LLMs may just be our fashion experts at the comfort of our own homes.
